Four funds - those returning 3, -2, -6, and -11 - were closed during the decade and no longer appear in the firm's lineup. Verify the advertisement.

arguments.code:
returns=[12,9,7,6,5,4,3,-2,-6,-11]
closed=[3,-2,-6,-11]
survivors=[r for r in returns if r not in closed]
sm=round(sum(survivors)/len(survivors),1); am=round(sum(returns)/len(returns),1)
print(f'survivor_mean={sm}')
print(f'all_funds_mean={am}')

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
survivor_mean=7.2
all_funds_mean=2.7

Verdict: 7.2% is the average of the survivors only. Deciding check: restore the dead to the average. The script separates the lineup: the six funds still open average 7.2%, exactly as advertised. All ten funds the firm actually ran average 2.7%. An investor choosing this firm a decade ago could not know which funds would survive; the return relevant to that decision is the all-funds figure, and the closures were not random - the firm closed its worst performers, which is precisely why the surviving average flatters it. This is survivorship bias in its most regulated, respectable form: no number is false, and the selection happens quietly through which entities still exist to be counted. The audit applies to fund league tables, index histories, and 'our customers' results' alike: ask what the population looked like at the start of the period, not at the end, and recompute the average over the original population.

A coding bootcamp advertises: '100% of our graduates are employed within six months.' Its cohort data: 480 students enrolled in the last class; 190 completed the program; all 190 completers found jobs. Assess the advertisement.

The claim is true of a minority of the people who paid. The deciding check is a cohort-definition audit: 'graduates' quietly replaces 'students.' Of the 480 who enrolled - the population a prospective student belongs to when deciding - 190 finished and found work, which is 39.6%. The other 290 students, who dropped out or were counseled out, vanish from the statistic entirely, and their outcomes (debt, months spent, jobs not obtained) are exactly what a buyer needs to know. Defining the denominator as completers is survivorship in a single word: any program, however poor, can approach a perfect placement rate by shedding enough students before graduation. The honest figure pairs both rates: completion rate and placement-among-completers, whose product is the chance an enrollee ends up employed. Audit rule: whenever a success rate is quoted for a program, ask 'of those who started.' If the source reports only finishers, assume the starting-cohort figure is the one they preferred you not to compute - and compute it.

A cookbook profiles 30 restaurants that opened in the fictional city of Sorrel in 2019 and are thriving five years later, drawing lessons about 'what makes a restaurant last.' City licensing records show 640 restaurants opened in Sorrel in 2019, and 118 were still operating in 2024. What context does the book omit?

The base rate that makes its lessons uninterpretable. Deciding check: survival-rate computation. Of the 640 restaurants that opened, 18.4% were still operating five years later - meaning the book's 30 profiles are drawn from a small surviving minority, and the 522 that closed are unavailable for interviews about their habits. If the closed restaurants also sourced locally, also had passionate chefs, also watched costs - as many surely did - then the book's 'lessons' describe the survivors' self-image, not the causes of survival. Worse, some traits may appear among survivors precisely because they are common among all restaurants, or even because risk-taking produces both spectacular success and most failures. None of this makes the profiles bad reading; it makes them bad evidence. The audit: before drawing lessons from any set of survivors - restaurants, startups, investors, dieters - establish what fraction survived and what the non-survivors looked like. Lessons drawn without the denominator are horoscopes with better production values.

Engineers at a fictional delivery-drone company examine their returned aircraft and find most weather damage on the underside and tail. They propose armoring those areas. A colleague objects. Using the evidence available, who is right and why?

The colleague is right, and the deciding check is asking which aircraft are missing from the dataset. The damage map describes only drones that came back. Drones hit in the underside and tail survived to be examined; the drones that never returned - the ones lost to weather - are absent from the hangar and from the data, and they were presumably lost because they were damaged in the places that prove fatal: the battery housing and rotors, which show little damage on the survivors precisely because damage there is not survivable. Armoring the areas with the most observed damage would protect against the injuries drones already withstand, while leaving the fatal vulnerabilities bare. The evidence, read naively, points in exactly the wrong direction. This is survivorship bias in physical form: the sample is filtered by the outcome (returning), so the data systematically omit the cases that matter most. The audit generalizes to any dataset of survivors - returned products, recovered aircraft, funds still trading, patients who completed a trial: before acting on the pattern, ask what the missing cases would show if they could report.

A sales-training company publishes 'Habits of Our Top 50 Reps,' based on interviewing the 50 highest sellers out of its 900-person sales force, and sells a course teaching the habits. Present a survivorship audit of the report in a table.

| Audit question | Finding | Implication |
|---|---|---|
| Who was sampled? | Top 50 of 900 reps (top 5.6%) | Extreme survivors only |
| Who is missing? | 850 reps, including any who used the same habits and failed | No comparison group |
| Were habits measured before or after success? | After, by self-report | Winners narrate causes; memory obliges |
| Base rate of the habits in the full force | Not reported | Habits may be universal, hence non-predictive |
| Verdict | Marketing document, not evidence | Course value unproven |

The table's decisive row is the fourth: a habit can only explain success if it is rarer among the unsuccessful, and this report never looks at the unsuccessful. If 800 of the 850 other reps also 'build relationships' and 'protect their mornings,' the top-50 interviews have identified the culture of the whole sales force, not the edge of its winners. The deciding check for all survivor research is identical: demand the trait's prevalence in the group that did not survive. A seller of the research who cannot or will not provide it is selling the survivors' autobiographies at course prices.

A review platform shows a fictional hotel, The Marlowe, at 4.6 stars from 1,000 reviews (total stars 4,600). A leaked moderation log shows the platform removed 210 one-star reviews of the hotel in a 'spam cleanup'; independent auditors found most were genuine guests. What was the hotel's average before the cleanup?

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content: restored_mean=4.0

Verdict: about 4.0 stars - the cleanup moved the hotel from mediocre to excellent. Deciding check: deleted-data restoration. Adding the 210 one-star reviews back gives 4,810 stars over 1,210 reviews, a mean of 4.0. Removing data is mathematically identical to adding flattering data: deleting a bloc of the worst observations raises every summary statistic while leaving the underlying experience untouched. Platforms have legitimate reasons to remove reviews - fraud is real - which is exactly why the audit cannot stop at 'some removals are justified.' The questions that matter are quantitative and procedural: how many were removed, from which end of the distribution, under what criteria, and with what effect on the displayed average. Any average computed over data that an interested party can prune should be treated as a lower bound on skepticism: ask for the removal count and restore the extremes to see whether the conclusion survives. Here it does not come close.

Two surveys released the same week seem to contradict each other on a proposed lakeside casino. Survey 1: 'Do you support banning the proposed casino?' - 38% say yes. Survey 2: 'Do you support restricting the proposed casino to the industrial zone with limited hours?' - 54% say yes. Commentators call public opinion 'confused and contradictory.' Is it?

The public is probably fine; the questions are different, and commentators compared the answers as if they were not. The deciding check is a question-wording comparison, and it should always precede theories about a fickle electorate. 'Banning' and 'restricting to a zone with limited hours' are different policies - a voter can coherently oppose a ban and favor restriction, or favor both, and the two surveys never asked the same population the same question, so there is no contradiction to explain. Apparent conflicts between polls dissolve remarkably often under this check: different verbs (ban/restrict/regulate), different objects (the casino/the casino's location), different premises smuggled into the preamble. Only after wording, population, and timing have been matched does a genuine disagreement remain for methodologists to argue about. Audit rule: when two sources conflict, align their instruments before their results. Most 'contradictions' in public data are two honest answers to two different questions, quoted as if they were one.

Two agencies report different jobless figures for the same region and month. Agency A: 6.1%. Agency B: 7.3%. The underlying counts: labor force 10,000; people without work and actively seeking it 610; 'discouraged' people who want work but stopped searching 130. Agency A counts only active seekers, in the labor force as defined. Agency B counts discouraged workers as jobless and adds them to both the jobless count and the labor force. Reconcile the two figures.

Verdict: both are arithmetically correct; they are measuring different definitions of joblessness. Deciding check: definition reconciliation. Agency A's rate is 6.1% - active seekers over the conventionally defined labor force. Agency B's is 7.3% - seekers plus discouraged workers over the expanded labor force. Neither agency erred, and the 1.2-point gap is not a dispute about the economy; it is a dispute about where the boundary of 'jobless' sits, which is a policy choice disguised as a measurement. Partisans will quote whichever figure suits the argument, and both will be 'official.' The audit when sources conflict is to obtain each one's numerator and denominator definitions and recompute both from shared counts, as here. If the figures reconcile under their definitions, the honest report presents both with their definitions attached. A conflict that survives definitional alignment is a real measurement problem; most do not survive it.

After a rally in a city plaza, the organizer claims 80,000 attended; police estimate 25,000; the transit authority reports 31,000 extra turnstile entries that day across nearby stations. The plaza's usable area is about 18,000 square meters, and crowd scientists use roughly 1.4 people per square meter for a dense but moving crowd. Which figure is most credible?

The police estimate, corroborated by two independent methods. The deciding check is an independent physical estimate: at a dense-crowd density of 1.4 people per square meter, the plaza holds about 25200 people - close to the police figure and physically incapable of holding 80,000, which would require more than four people per square meter sustained across the whole plaza, a crush density no rally maintains. The turnstile count points the same way: 31,000 extra entries is an upper bound on arrivals by transit, consistent with a crowd in the mid-twenties of thousands once walkers and drivers are added, and inconsistent with 80,000. Note the structure of the disagreement: the organizer's number is produced by an interested party with no stated method, while the two lower figures come from methods (area times density, turnstile counts) that can be examined and rerun. When sources conflict, do not average them and do not count them; weigh the ones with checkable methods. Interested estimates are evidence mainly about what the interested party wishes were true.

Two analytics firms report different quarterly sales for the same retailer. Firm X: $1.24M. Firm Y: $0.97M. The retailer's ledger shows gross bookings of $1,240,000, returns of $190,000, and cancelled orders of $80,000. Firm X reports bookings; Firm Y reports sales net of returns and cancellations. Who is right?

arguments.code:
bookings=1240000; returns=190000; cancels=80000
net=bookings-returns-cancels
gap=bookings-net
print(f'net_sales={net}')
print(f'gap={gap}')
print(f'gap_pct_of_gross={round(100*gap/bookings,1)}')

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
net_sales=970000
gap=270000
gap_pct_of_gross=21.8

Both - about different quantities. Deciding check: gross-versus-net definition reconciliation. The script nets the ledger out: $970000 in completed, kept sales, and the entire disagreement is the $270000 of returns and cancellations, 21.8% of gross. Firm X's number answers 'how much was ordered'; Firm Y's answers 'how much money stayed.' For judging the retailer's health, the net figure is the meaningful one - a store can grow bookings while drowning in returns - but for judging demand or warehouse load, gross is informative. Conflicts like this are rarely resolved by picking a winner; they are resolved by naming the quantity. The audit: when two credible sources give different figures for 'the same' quantity, suspect definitions before dishonesty, and obtain the bridge - the list of inclusions and exclusions that converts one figure into the other. A source that cannot produce its bridge is guessing; a source that will not is selling.

A headline reads: 'Ten studies link the sweetener Zylane to headaches; only two find no effect - science is split 10 to 2.' Details in the article: the ten positive studies are small observational surveys with a combined enrollment of 1,340; the two null studies are preregistered randomized trials with a combined enrollment of 48,000. Is 'split 10 to 2' a fair summary?

It counts studies the way a show of hands counts arguments - one each, regardless of weight. The deciding check is weighting by method and scale rather than tallying conclusions. The ten positive results come from small observational surveys, a design that cannot separate the sweetener from everything else headache-prone people do, and whose combined enrollment is 1,340. The two null results come from preregistered randomized trials - the design built precisely to answer causal questions, with hypotheses and analyses fixed in advance - enrolling 48,000 people between them. On any sane weighting, the evidence leans strongly toward 'no effect,' and the 10-to-2 framing inverts it. Vote-counting fails because publication is not random: small positive studies are easier to publish and publicize than small null ones, so raw tallies overcount exactly the weakest evidence. The audit: for any 'studies disagree' story, list each study's design and size before its conclusion. A literature is a weighted body of evidence, not a legislature, and it should never be summarized by a show of hands.

Three sources give three 'average rents' for the same city in the same month: a listings site says $1,850; a household survey says $1,420; a student-housing report says $960. Present a reconciliation table explaining how all three can be right.

| Source | Population | Definition | Figure | Why it differs |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Listings site | Apartments currently advertised | Asking rent, new leases | $1,850 | Asking prices for vacant units; skews to newer, pricier stock |
| Household survey | All renting households | Rent actually paid, all leases | $1,420 | Includes long-term tenants on old, below-market leases |
| Student report | Student rentals only | Rent per bed, shared units | $960 | Per-person share of shared housing, not per unit |

Verdict: no source is wrong, and no two are measuring the same thing. The deciding check is a population-and-definition alignment: each figure is correct for its population (advertised units, all tenants, students) and its unit (per lease signed now, per lease in force, per bed). The conflict exists only in the headlines, which strip the qualifiers and present three different quantities as rival estimates of one quantity. This is the most common genus of statistical disagreement in public life - not fraud, not error, but definitional drift amplified by compression. The remedy is unglamorous: refuse to compare figures until population, unit, and time window are matched, and treat any 'average X' quoted without those three attachments as a number waiting for its meaning.

Two climate summaries for the fictional Meridian Valley weather station conflict. One says the valley has warmed 0.98 degrees since 1950; the other says 0.68 degrees since 1980. The station's decadal anomalies (degrees, relative to a fixed reference): 1950: -0.12; 1980: +0.18; 2020: +0.86. Both summaries cite this station. Reconcile them.

Verdict: both are correct subtractions over different windows. Deciding check: baseline-period audit. From 1950 to 2020 the change is 0.98 degrees; from 1980 it is 0.68 degrees. The summaries do not disagree about a single temperature reading; they disagree about when the story starts, and the start date does argumentative work - 1950 captures the full post-war warming, 1980 starts after a chunk of it already happened. Baseline selection is the trend version of the base-year trick in sales claims, and it is just as mechanical to audit: obtain the underlying series, recompute the change over several plausible windows, and notice which window each advocate chose. A source confident in its case reports the long window and lets shorter ones fall where they may. When a trend claim arrives without its start date's justification - or when the start date coincides suspiciously with a local peak or trough - the window, not the data, is the message.

Two polls in the same week put a ballot measure's support at 52% (live phone interviews, registered voters, n = 900) and 44% (online opt-in panel, adults who say they are 'very likely' to vote, n = 2,400). A columnist writes that 'the race is volatile and voters are swinging wildly.' Better explanation?

Measurement changed more than minds did. The deciding check is a method diff: before attributing a gap to the electorate, list everything that differs between the instruments. Here that is nearly everything - mode (live phone versus opt-in online), population (registered voters versus self-described very likely voters), and recruitment (probability dialing versus volunteers). Each difference is worth points on its own: opt-in panels over-represent the politically engaged, 'very likely' self-screens over-represent the committed, and phone and online respondents answer sensitive questions differently. An 8-point gap across this many simultaneous changes is unremarkable and carries almost no information about movement, which can only be tracked by the same firm, same method, same population over time. The columnist's 'wild swings' narrative is what happens when method variance is read as opinion variance. Audit rule: two numbers are comparable only to the extent their methods are identical. When methods differ, the honest story is about the instruments, and any claim of volatility is speculation wearing data's clothing.

A newspaper ranks two hospitals by raw mortality: Hospital A, 84 deaths among 2,000 patients (4.2%); Hospital B, 62 among 2,000 (3.1%) - and calls B the safer hospital. A health authority objects: A's patients are far sicker on arrival. Given each hospital's case mix, expected deaths were 5.1% of patients at A and 2.6% at B. Work out the risk-adjusted comparison (standardized mortality ratio = observed / expected).

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
hospital_A_raw_pct=4.2
hospital_A_smr=0.82
hospital_B_raw_pct=3.1
hospital_B_smr=1.19

Verdict: the ranking reverses under risk adjustment. Deciding check: compare observed deaths with case-mix-expected deaths, not with the other hospital's raw rate. The script computes each hospital's standardized mortality ratio: A's is 0.82 - it lost 18% fewer patients than its case mix predicts - while B's is 1.19, 19% more deaths than expected. Hospital A takes the trauma transfers, the late-stage cancers, the patients other facilities cannot treat; its raw 4.2% mortality reflects who arrives, not how they are treated, and B's lower raw 3.1% reflects a healthier intake. Raw-rate league tables systematically punish exactly the institutions that accept the hardest cases, and can push hospitals to avoid sick patients - the metric corrupts the mission. The audit generalizes to school test scores, surgeon ratings, and police clearance rates: whenever outcomes depend on intake difficulty, demand the adjusted figure and the expected baseline it was computed against. An unadjusted ranking of unlike caseloads is not a simplification; it is a different, wrong answer.

A news segment on a bridge-safety review gives equal time to 'both sides': engineers who endorse the inspection regime and two engineers who call it inadequate. The segment says 'engineers remain divided.' The professional survey cited in the same segment polled 214 structural engineers; 2 expressed the critical view. Fair framing?

No - 'divided' describes a split the numbers do not show. The deciding check is counting the sides: the critical position is held by 0.9% of the surveyed engineers, 2 of 214. Presenting one spokesperson per side manufactures a 50-50 visual for a 99-to-1 reality, and viewers reliably take the format's word over the statistic's. False balance is not neutrality; it is a distortion that systematically inflates fringe positions, because the fringe is the only side that benefits from equal time. The honest format weights voices by their prevalence in the relevant expert population while still reporting that dissent exists and what it argues - the two critics may even be right, and their arguments deserve a hearing on their merits. What they do not deserve is a headcount they do not have. Audit rule: whenever coverage says experts are 'divided,' 'split,' or 'debating,' find the actual distribution - a survey, a literature tally, a professional body's position. If the split is 99 to 1, the story is the consensus and the interesting question is why the 1% dissents, not whether a debate exists.

A publisher's announcement celebrates: 'One million copies sold in the first year!' Its distribution report shows 1,000,000 copies shipped to retailers and 310,000 copies returned unsold under the industry's returns system. What did the book actually sell?

Verdict: 690000 copies - a strong result that did not need the inflation. Deciding check: shipped-versus-sold reconciliation. In publishing, 'shipped' counts books sent to stores; 'sold' should count books that left stores in customers' hands and stayed there. Returns are 31.0% of shipments here, and every returned copy was counted in the million and then quietly un-happened. The announcement exploits a vocabulary gap: the industry uses 'sold' for 'sold into the channel' while readers hear 'sold to readers,' and the 310,000-copy difference lives in that gap. The same genus of trick appears wherever goods move through intermediaries - 'sales' that are factory shipments, 'subscribers' that are free trials, 'downloads' that are pre-installs. The audit: for any sales claim through a channel, ask what the returns, refunds, or churn figures are, and subtract them before repeating the number. A source that reports gross without net, in an industry with material returns, has chosen the larger number on purpose.

A tutoring company, Bright Ladder, reports: 'Students using our method gain an average of 21 percentile points; 94% of families renew.' Its report is based on students who completed the full two-year program: 310 of the 780 who enrolled. A rival analysis of the same company, counting all enrollees and comparing against matched students at ordinary tutoring, estimates the gain at 6 points. Present an audit table.

| Check | Finding | Effect on the claim |
|---|---|---|
| Denominator | 310 completers of 780 enrolled | 60% of students excluded - survivorship |
| Who drops out | Not reported | Struggling students plausibly over-represented among leavers |
| Comparison group | None in company report; rival uses matched controls | Company's 21 points includes maturation and practice effects |
| Renewal figure | 94% of completers renew | Renewal among survivors is near-tautological |
| Rival estimate | 6 points, all enrollees, controlled | Different population and method, not a contradiction |

Verdict: the company's numbers may be accurate descriptions of its completers and are useless as predictions for an enrollee. The deciding pattern is survivorship compounded by a missing control: students who persist for two years in any tutoring gain ground from growing older, practicing tests, and being the kind of students who persist. The rival's 6 points is not 'the truth' either - matching is imperfect - but it answers the question a parent is actually asking: what does enrollment add, for a child who enrolls? Audit rule: for program claims, insist on the enrolled-cohort figure with a comparison group, and treat completer-only statistics as advertising copy regardless of how carefully they were compiled.

A clinic's promotional video features 7 patients who recovered remarkably from a chronic condition after treatment there. The clinic has treated about 3,000 patients with the condition. The condition's own literature (quoted in the clinic's intake packet) notes that about 0.5% of patients experience a marked spontaneous improvement in any given year, treatment aside. Evaluate the video's evidence.

The featured recoveries are fewer than chance alone predicts. The deciding check is an expected-count computation: at a 0.5% spontaneous improvement rate across 3,000 patients, about 15 patients would be expected to improve markedly in a year with no effective treatment at all. The clinic showcases 7 - half the number the base rate generates for free. This does not prove the treatment fails; the clinic's overall outcomes might still exceed the base rate, and the video is a selection of stories, not an outcome registry. But as evidence, the video is worse than neutral: it demonstrates that the clinic can find seven good stories in a population where roughly fifteen were guaranteed to exist. Testimonial evidence feels decisive because faces and voices are vivid, and it is structurally incapable of carrying the weight placed on it - the denominator is invisible, the selection is by the seller, and the base rate does the real explanatory work. The audit for any 'meet our successes' presentation: multiply the base rate by the total served and compare with the number showcased. If chance predicts more successes than are shown, you are watching marketing arithmetic, not results.

A researcher is pleased: her paper was accepted by the 'Calder Annals of Medicine,' which she believes is the long-established 'Annals of Calder Medicine.' The acceptance came from a lookalike website with a similar logo. How can she, and readers, tell the journals apart?

By identifiers, not names - journal names are unprotected text, and mimicking a respected title is the oldest trick in predatory publishing. The deciding check is identity verification through registries: the established journal has a long-held ISSN, a decades-deep archive in the standard indexes, a named editorial board at real institutions, and a publisher with a traceable catalog. The lookalike has a recently registered ISSN (or none), an archive that begins last year, board members who cannot be found at their stated institutions, and a website that appeared recently despite claiming a long history. Hijacked and imitative journals harvest both fees and credibility: authors pay to publish, and the paper then circulates wearing the real journal's reputation, misleading every reader who does not check. The audit takes minutes: look the ISSN up in the registry, confirm the journal appears in the indexes it claims, and verify one or two board members independently. Any claim resting on 'published in the X journal' deserves the same check - the name is the claim's packaging, and packaging is exactly what predators counterfeit.

Score this journal from its own website and solicitation email. Facts: it promises 'peer review completed within 5 days'; charges a $1,650 article processing fee payable before review begins; its stated scope covers 'all fields of science, medicine, engineering, and humanities'; its editorial board lists 3 people with no institutional affiliations; it advertises a 'Global Impact Factor of 7.9' from an unrecognized metrics firm; the editor's invitation arrived as bulk email praising the recipient's unrelated past paper; no publisher address is given; it does not appear in the standard journal indexes it name-drops. Present a scorecard.

| Tell | Present? | Weight |
|---|---|---|
| Review promised in 5 days | Yes | Real review of a paper takes weeks to months |
| Fee demanded before review | Yes | Revenue depends on acceptance, not quality |
| Scope covers everything | Yes | No scholarly community actually served |
| Board without affiliations | Yes | Unverifiable or fictitious governance |
| Invented impact metric | Yes | 'Global Impact Factor' is not a recognized measure |
| Spam solicitation flattering unrelated work | Yes | Author is the customer being hunted |
| No publisher address; false indexing claims | Yes | No accountable institution behind the title |
| Verdict | Predatory - do not submit, do not cite as peer-reviewed | - |

No single row is proof - legitimate new journals can be small, fast, or broad - but predatory operations fail in patterns because their business model (collect fees, publish everything) forces every one of these tells at once. The deciding check is the pattern, weighted heaviest on the two rows that reveal the model: payment before review, and review timelines incompatible with review. A journal whose income requires acceptance cannot perform rejection, and a journal that cannot reject is not a journal but a printing service with an ISSN. Papers published there should be read as unreviewed manuscripts, whatever the website calls them.

A doctoral student receives an email: her 40-page manuscript has been 'accepted with minor revisions' by a journal three days after submission, with an invoice attached and a request to pay within a week to 'secure the slot.' Reviewer comments consist of two generic sentences. She is thrilled. Should she be?

She should be alarmed - the timeline alone refutes the process. The deciding check is a review-feasibility audit: genuine peer review requires recruiting two or three qualified, busy strangers, who must read 40 pages critically and write reports; even an efficient journal measures this in weeks, and the two generic sentences supplied are not reports any expert would write about real work. Three days including a weekend means the manuscript was, at most, skimmed by someone whose job is to accept it. The invoice timing completes the picture: payment demanded before publication, under deadline pressure ('secure the slot'), reveals the customer relationship - the journal sells acceptances, and its haste is a sales technique, since delay invites second thoughts. Publishing there is worse than not publishing: the paper becomes permanently associated with a venue that informed readers discount to zero, and the work can rarely be republished in a legitimate journal afterward. Audit rule: any acceptance faster than a careful read of the manuscript is possible is not an acceptance; it is a receipt.

A journal advertises an impact factor of 7.9. Its own archive shows it published 96 papers across the two preceding years, and a citation database counts 214 citations to those papers in the current year. The standard impact-factor definition is: citations in the current year to the previous two years' papers, divided by the number of those papers. Compute the journal's actual figure.

Verdict: the journal's real impact factor is 2.2, and the advertised 7.9 is fabricated. Deciding check: recompute the metric from its definition and the journal's own counts. Two hundred fourteen citations over 96 papers gives 2.2 - a respectable-enough figure for a small journal, which makes the inflation to 7.9 a pure credibility purchase. Predatory and marginal journals favor fake metrics because the impact factor is the one number authors are trained to chase, and because most readers never recompute it; the metric's authority comes from a specific producer using a specific formula, and lookalike figures ('Global Impact Factor,' 'Universal Impact Factor') borrow the name while answering to nobody. The audit generalizes to every composite metric - rankings, scores, ratings: find the definition, find the raw counts, redo the division. A metric that cannot survive its own definition being applied to its publisher's own data is not a metric; it is a logo.

A journal's website lists a distinguished editorial board of 14. A librarian checking it finds: 5 members are listed with no institution; 2 have names matching professors who died several years ago; the editor-in-chief's listed university has no record of her; and 3 members, when emailed by the librarian, reply that they have never heard of the journal. What has the librarian established?

That the board is set dressing. The deciding check is editorial-board verification: a journal's board is its governance made visible, and each member is an independently checkable claim - a real person, at a real institution, who has agreed to serve. This board fails in every direction at once: unverifiable affiliations, deceased members who cannot have consented, an editor whose institution disowns her, and listed members who deny involvement. Predatory journals assemble boards by copying names from real journals' mastheads, because a plausible board is the fastest way to look legitimate to a hurried author. The deeper point is that board fraud is diagnostic of everything else: an operation willing to counterfeit its governance will not perform real peer review, real editing, or real archiving either. The audit is cheap and decisive - pick three board members at random and verify them through their institutions' own pages, not the journal's links. One denial is a clerical error; a pattern of them is the journal's true peer review, conducted by you, and the paper fails it.

A headline announces: 'Compound L improves memory in older adults, study finds.' The cited study enrolled 44 university students aged 18-22, kept them awake for 30 hours, and measured reaction time on a vigilance task after giving Compound L or placebo. List the mismatches between headline and study.

Three, and each alone would sink the headline. The deciding check is a claim-versus-citation match on population, outcome, and condition. Population: the headline says older adults; the study tested 18-to-22-year-olds, whose brains, baselines, and reasons for impairment differ categorically. Outcome: the headline says memory; the study measured reaction time on a vigilance task - related to alertness, not to remembering anything. Condition: the study's impairment was acute sleep deprivation, an artificial state; nothing was tested about ordinary aging, ordinary sleep, or the chronic use a reader would contemplate. What the study actually supports is narrow: Compound L partly offset reaction-time slowing in sleep-deprived students. Every word the headline changed - memory for reaction time, older adults for students, improvement for partial rescue of an induced deficit - widened the claim toward the audience most likely to buy the compound. The audit is mechanical: extract the headline's population, outcome, and setting, then extract the same three from the cited abstract. If any of the three differs, the citation does not support the claim, full stop.

A magazine reports: 'Heavy screen users show anxiety at 25.5%, versus 15.3% for light users - screens are driving the anxiety epidemic.' The underlying survey counts, split by age: teens, heavy users 90 anxious of 300, light users 28 of 100; adults, heavy users 12 of 100, light users 33 of 300. Examine the claim within age groups.

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
teens_high=30.0
teens_low=28.0
adults_high=12.0
adults_low=11.0
overall_high=25.5
overall_low=15.25

Verdict: within each age group the association nearly vanishes; the headline effect is manufactured by mixing populations. Deciding check: stratified recomputation. The script computes the group rates: teens, heavy 30.0% versus light 28.0% - a 2-point gap. Adults, heavy 12.0% versus light 11.0% - a 1-point gap. But teens are both more anxious and more likely to be heavy users, so pooling the groups loads the heavy-user column with teens and produces the alarming 25.5% versus 15.25% contrast. Age is doing the work that the headline assigns to screens. This is confounding, the standing hazard of every observational 'X linked to Y' claim, and stratification is its standard antidote: recompute the association inside homogeneous slices of the obvious third variables. A real effect usually survives slicing, perhaps weakened; an artifact dissolves, as here. The audit for any pooled association: ask what third factor predicts both sides, then demand the sliced numbers. If a source reports only the pooled figure, it is showing you the version most likely to mislead.

A news headline states: 'Coffee causes improved liver markers, researchers find.' The study's abstract concludes: 'Coffee consumption was associated with more favorable liver enzyme levels in this cross-sectional sample.' The study measured coffee intake and liver markers once, at the same time, in 2,300 adults. What is the problem?

The headline upgraded the study's verb, and the design cannot pay for the upgrade. The deciding check is an abstract-versus-headline verb audit backed by design: the researchers wrote 'was associated with,' the standard hedge for an observational correlation, and the headline replaced it with 'causes.' A cross-sectional study - everything measured once, simultaneously - cannot establish causation even in principle: it cannot show which came first (perhaps people with liver concerns were advised to drink coffee, or a third factor, like income or medication, drives both), and its own authors declined to claim otherwise. The distance between 'associated' and 'causes' is the distance between a hypothesis and a conclusion, and headline writers cross it because causal claims are news and correlations are not. The audit costs nothing: read the abstract's conclusion sentence and compare its verbs with the headline's. Where they differ, believe the abstract - it survived peer review, while the headline survived an editor optimizing for clicks. A source that routinely strengthens verbs is telling you its claims are worth one grade less than printed.

An article states that mineral supplement Ossavin 'is supported by the literature,' citing a 2024 review. Tracing the review's reference list, its sole citation for the Ossavin claim is a 2023 commentary - whose author is Ossavin's manufacturer-funded researcher - and the commentary in turn cites 'emerging clinical literature,' naming the very review articles that cite it. What has the tracing established?

That the literature support is a loop with no data in it. The deciding check is citation-graph tracing: follow each citation to its source until you reach either primary data or a dead end, and watch for the path circling back. Here every route terminates in a commentary by an interested author, which itself points forward to the reviews that point back to it - a closed circuit in which each document borrows authority from the next and none contributes a measurement. Circular citation is more common than outright fabrication because it assembles itself innocently: a commentary speculates, a review cites the speculation as a source, an article cites the review as 'the literature,' and after two hops the claim wears the costume of consensus. The number of citing documents grows impressively while the evidence remains exactly one opinion. The audit is laborious but definitive: for any 'supported by the literature' claim, pick the strongest citation and walk it to ground. If the ground is data, the claim has a floor; if the ground is another citation, keep walking; if the walk returns to its starting point, the claim has no floor at all.

A researcher's profile boasts that her key paper has been 'cited by 300 papers.' A bibliometric breakdown of those 300 citations: 96 are self-citations by the paper's own authors in their later work; 41 are duplicate records, errata notices, and citation-index artifacts rather than substantive citing papers. How many independent external citations remain?

Verdict: 163 - a solid count that did not need the padding. Deciding check: citation-count decomposition. Raw citation totals aggregate things of very different evidentiary value: a citation from an independent group replicating or building on the work is a vote of confidence; a self-citation is the authors citing themselves, which is normal scholarly practice but is not external validation; a duplicate or erratum record is a database artifact that validates nothing. Subtracting the self-citations and artifacts leaves 163 genuine external citations, the number that actually measures the paper's reception by its field. The audit mirrors the shipped-versus-sold correction in commerce: gross counts are chosen because they are larger, and the decomposition is unglamorous arithmetic anyone can do when the breakdown is available. Where it is not available, treat round, boasted citation counts as marketing figures. Citation counts measure attention, not correctness, in any case - but if a count is to be used at all, it should at least count what it claims to count.

Audit three claims from a health newsletter against the sources they cite. Claim 1: 'Fasting reverses insulin resistance' - cited source: a mouse study showing improved insulin markers after fasting. Claim 2: 'Our city's tap water meets all safety standards' - cited source: the municipal water authority's annual compliance report, which lists every regulated contaminant within limits. Claim 3: 'Standing desks burn 300 extra calories a day' - cited source: a study measuring 34 extra calories per hour of standing over a 3-hour observation, in 23 office workers. Present a citation-support table.

| Claim | What the cited source actually shows | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| Fasting reverses insulin resistance | Improved insulin markers in mice; no human reversal measured | Does not support - species and strength both exceed the source |
| Tap water meets all standards | Full contaminant panel within regulatory limits, from the responsible authority | Supports - primary source, claim matches scope |
| Standing desks burn 300 extra calories/day | 34 extra calories per hour over 3 hours in 23 workers | Partially supports direction; the 300 figure requires ~9 hours of standing, far beyond the study |

The table's middle row matters as much as the failures: citation auditing is not a machine for debunking, and a claim matched to a primary source at the right scope should be credited. The failures fail in the two classic directions - the fasting claim borrows a stronger conclusion ('reverses') and a different species than its source, while the standing-desk claim keeps the source's direction but extrapolates its small, short measurement across an unrealistic day. The deciding check is uniform: state what the source shows in one sentence, state the claim in one sentence, and compare them word by word. Most citation abuse is visible in that single side-by-side.

A 2026 article supports its argument with a 2019 study. Checking the study's page reveals a retraction notice dated 2023: the journal retracted the paper after an investigation found fabricated data in two figures. The 2026 article does not mention the retraction. How should the article's claim be treated?

As unsupported - its only cited foundation was formally withdrawn. The deciding check is a retraction-status lookup, the cheapest audit in all of source evaluation: before relying on any study, check whether it still stands. Retraction is science's formal mechanism for unpublishing work found to be fraudulent or fatally erroneous, and a retracted paper is not 'controversial' or 'one side of a debate'; it is a document the record has disowned. Yet retracted studies continue to accumulate supportive citations for years, because citing authors copy references from other bibliographies without visiting the source - citation decay again, this time preserving a corpse. The 2026 article's failure may be laziness rather than malice, but the effect on a reader is identical: a claim presented as evidence-based rests on fabricated data. Practical rule: any study load-bearing in an argument gets a ten-second status check on its journal page or a retraction database. If it has been retracted, the citing article's claim reverts to assertion, and every other citation in that article deserves a second look - an author who missed a retraction notice was not reading their sources closely.

A trial of a fictional pain gel reports in its abstract: 'The gel significantly improved outcome scores (p = 0.041).' The trial's registry entry lists 14 pre-specified outcome measures. The full results table gives these p-values for the 14 outcomes: 0.31, 0.08, 0.42, 0.19, 0.041, 0.67, 0.23, 0.55, 0.12, 0.89, 0.36, 0.28, 0.74, 0.61. Assess the abstract's claim.

arguments.code:
pvals=[0.31,0.08,0.42,0.19,0.041,0.67,0.23,0.55,0.12,0.89,0.36,0.28,0.74,0.61]
sig=sum(1 for p in pvals if p<0.05)
print(f'outcomes_tested={len(pvals)}')
print(f'significant={sig}')
print(f'expected_by_chance={round(len(pvals)*0.05,1)}')

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
outcomes_tested=14
significant=1
expected_by_chance=0.7

Verdict: the abstract reports the lottery's winning ticket and omits the other thirteen tickets. Deciding check: outcome-count versus reported-count. The script tallies the full table: 14 outcomes tested, 1 significant at the 5% level, and 0.7 significant results expected from an ineffective treatment purely by chance. One marginal hit at p = 0.041 - barely under the wire - among fourteen tries is the null hypothesis's signature, not a discovery. The registry entry is what makes this audit possible: because the outcomes were pre-specified publicly, the reader can count the denominator the abstract hides. Without registration, the same maneuver is invisible, which is why registration exists. The audit for any trial claim: find the registry entry or protocol, count the pre-specified outcomes, and compare with the number the abstract celebrates. A treatment that 'works' on one of fourteen measures, at p = 0.041, has not been shown to work; it has been shown to have been tested fourteen times.

An author's CV lists a paper in the 'International Journal of Emerging Engineering Research.' Checking the publication: it has an ISBN rather than an ISSN, it is the proceedings volume of a commercial conference, papers were accepted after a single organizer review, and the 'journal' is not in any scholarly index. What is this publication, really?

It is a conference proceedings volume wearing a journal's name. The deciding check is publication-type verification: journals carry ISSNs and publish in issues over time under an editorial board; conference proceedings carry ISBNs, appear once per event, and are edited by the event's organizers. The distinction is not pedantry - 'peer-reviewed journal article' and 'conference paper accepted by the organizer' certify very different amounts of scrutiny, and CVs, tenure files, and product claims all spend the former's credibility. Commercial conference mills exploit the ambiguity deliberately: journal-style names, journal-style websites, and proceedings that let attendees claim a publication for the price of a registration fee. The tells are consistent: ISBN instead of ISSN, acceptance tied to event registration, a single annual volume, no indexing, no archive beyond the event. The audit takes one search: look up the title in an ISSN registry and a scholarly index. If a 'journal' cannot be found in either, everything published under its name should be weighted as unreviewed - including when the person citing it is the one who published there.

A journal advertises itself as 'rigorously peer-reviewed.' Its author guidelines state: authors must suggest three reviewers and provide their email addresses; the journal 'typically decides within 6 days'; no editor is named anywhere on the site; reviewer reports are not shared with authors. Evaluate the peer-review claim.

The described process is peer review in name only. The deciding check is a review-model audit: examine how reviewers are chosen, by whom, and with what accountability. Author-suggested reviewers contacted at author-supplied addresses is the classic mechanism of review fraud - the 'reviewers' are routinely the authors' colleagues, or the authors themselves behind fresh email accounts - and any journal using it without independent verification has outsourced its quality control to the people being controlled. The six-day decision window confirms it: real reviewers cannot be recruited, read a paper, and report in six days as a routine matter. The absence of a named editor means no accountable person stands behind any decision. Legitimate journals differ in their models - single-blind, double-blind, open reports - but they share the load-bearing features: the journal selects reviewers independently, an identifiable editor owns the decision, and timelines are measured in weeks. When a venue's process omits those features, its 'peer-reviewed' label is a claim about marketing, and work published there should be read as unreviewed manuscripts with better typography.

A drug advertisement claims the medication 'cuts cardiac risk,' citing its trial. The trial's headline result is an 18% improvement in a blood biomarker. The trial's table for actual cardiac events: 41 events among 400 patients on the drug; 43 among 400 on placebo. Evaluate the advertisement against the trial's primary clinical outcome.

Verdict: on the outcome that matters to patients, the trial shows essentially nothing. Deciding check: primary-outcome versus surrogate substitution. The event rates are 10.25% on the drug and 10.75% on placebo - a difference of 0.5 percentage points, two events in 400 patients, well within noise. The advertisement instead quotes the 18% biomarker improvement, because biomarkers move more easily than diseases do. A surrogate endpoint is a stand-in - a lab value believed to track the real outcome - and stand-ins can improve while patients do not, a pattern behind some of medicine's most expensive disappointments. The trial may have been designed around the biomarker honestly; the advertisement's move is presenting the surrogate as if it were the clinical result. The audit: for any treatment claim, find the primary clinical outcome - events, deaths, symptoms, function - and read its numbers before any biomarker. If the marketing leads with a surrogate and the clinical outcome is buried or absent, assume the clinical outcome disappointed. That assumption, like most in this field, is a bet the evidence usually pays out.

Perform a full audit of this claim from a fictional supplement, Verdana Root Extract: 'Clinically shown to improve joint mobility by 30%.' Facts available: the cited 'clinical study' is a company-run survey of 62 customers with no control group; the 30% figure is the average self-reported improvement among the 41 customers who completed the survey; the product page's citation is to the company's own white paper; the claim is repeated by two affiliate blogs that cite the product page. Present a five-check audit table.

| Check | Finding | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Source type | Company white paper, not a published study | Fails - 'clinically shown' unsupported |
| Design | No control group; self-reported outcomes | Fails - placebo effect and natural fluctuation unmeasured |
| Denominator | 41 completers of 62 surveyed | Fails - a third of respondents vanished from the average |
| Independence of corroboration | Two blogs cite the product page itself | Fails - circular, zero independent sources |
| Effect plausibility | 30% average improvement, no variance reported | Unverifiable - no distribution, no raw data |

Verdict: the claim fails every check it can be put to, and the failures are independent - fixing any one would not rescue it. This is the signature of a manufactured claim: it is not a good study summarized badly, but a marketing sentence with a citation-shaped decoration. The deciding pattern across the table is that every road back to evidence ends at the seller: the study is theirs, the paper is theirs, the corroboration is their own page echoed by affiliates. Genuine evidence has at least one link in the chain that the claimant does not control. Audit rule: trace a claim's chain and mark each link's owner. If the claimant owns every link, the claim is an assertion with footnotes, and should be priced as one.

An article states: 'A peer-reviewed study in a leading journal has found that microplastic exposure alters gut bacteria.' The link leads to a preprint server page, where a banner reads 'This is a preliminary report that has not yet been peer reviewed,' posted five weeks ago. Assess the article's description.

The description is false in both of its load-bearing words. The deciding check is publication-status verification: the document is a preprint - a manuscript posted publicly before review - and its own page says so in a banner the article's author either missed or ignored. It is not peer-reviewed, and it is not in a journal, leading or otherwise. Preprints are a legitimate and valuable part of modern science: they speed up sharing, and many are later published in revised form. But their findings carry a preliminary status precisely because no independent experts have yet checked the methods, and a meaningful share are substantially changed or never published. Citing a preprint as peer-reviewed strips the one caveat that defines it. The audit is nearly free: click the link. If the landing page is a preprint server (the banner, the DOI prefix, the 'preprint' label), downgrade every claim drawn from it to 'unreviewed manuscript reports,' and check back later for the published version, whose numbers may differ. An article that upgrades a preprint's status has failed the easiest check in this entire discipline.

An article on a fictional arthritis cream reports: 'In trials, the cream improved mobility by 2.4% over control.' The trial measured the mobility difference at four timepoints: week 2: -1.2%; week 4: -0.8%; week 6: +2.4%; week 8: -0.6%. Evaluate the article's choice of figure.

arguments.code:
effects=[('week 2',-1.2),('week 4',-0.8),('week 6',2.4),('week 8',-0.6)]
for w,v in effects: print(f'{w}={v}')
mean=round(sum(v for _,v in effects)/len(effects),2)
print(f'mean_effect={mean}')

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
week 2=-1.2
week 4=-0.8
week 6=2.4
week 8=-0.6
mean_effect=-0.05

Verdict: the article quoted the single favorable reading out of four. Deciding check: full time-course versus single timepoint. The script lists the series: the cream trails control at weeks -1.2 and -0.8, spikes to +2.4 at week 6, and falls back to -0.6 by week 8. The mean effect across the trial is -0.05% - indistinguishable from nothing. A lone positive blip in a noisy series is what randomness produces; selecting it afterward and presenting it as 'the trial's result' converts noise into a finding. The week-6 figure is not fabricated, which is what makes the maneuver durable: every number in the article is real, and only the selection is dishonest. The audit: for any result quoted from a repeated-measures study, demand the whole series - all timepoints, all doses, all subgroups that were measured. Effects that are real tend to persist across neighboring measurements; effects that exist at exactly one point, surrounded by nulls and negatives, are weather, not climate.

A wellness article about the fictional berry 'luma fruit' makes four claims. (1) 'Luma exports grew 64% last year, showing surging demand' - the trade table reads: exports were 340 tonnes two years ago and 121 tonnes last year (both complete years); the article's 64% comes from comparing a partial current-year figure of 199 tonnes against last year's 121. (2) 'Studies show luma improves sleep' - the only citation is the Luma Growers Association's own survey. (3) 'Luma extract improved memory in a clinical trial' - the trial tested reaction time in sleep-deprived students. (4) 'Luma juice contains 42 mg of vitamin C per serving' - from the national food-composition database's entry for the fruit. Audit all four.

Claim by claim, each fails or passes on a different check. (1) Demand surge: fails the like-for-like window check. Comparing a partial current year against a full prior year is meaningless; the last two complete years show exports falling from 340 to 121 tonnes, a change of -64.4% - demand, on the article's own chosen evidence, collapsed. (2) Sleep: fails the citation-existence and independence checks - the sole source is the growers' own association survey, an interested party, so 'studies show' reduces to 'the seller says.' (3) Memory: fails the claim-versus-citation match - the trial measured reaction time, not memory, in sleep-deprived students, not the article's general readership; population and outcome both mismatch. (4) Vitamin C: passes - a national food-composition database is a primary reference source, the claim is a straightforward composition fact within its scope, and 42 mg is checkable by any reader in seconds. The set is a fair sample of the wild: three failures by three different mechanisms and one clean pass. That is why the audits must be plural - no single check catches everything, and the discipline is a checklist, not an instinct.
